title: Decorators
description: How decorators work as functions that wrap other functions, the @ syntax, and practical use cases.
objectives: Understand that functions are objects that can be passed around and wrapped
Write and apply a decorator using @ syntax
Handle arguments and return values correctly inside a decorator
Stack multiple decorators on one function

content.heading: Functions as Objects and the Decorator Pattern
content.body:
Because Python functions are first-class objects, a function can accept another function as an argument, and return a function as its result. A decorator is exactly this pattern applied to modify or extend a function's behavior without changing its source code: a decorator function takes a function, defines an inner wrapper function that adds behavior around a call to the original, and returns that wrapper. The @decorator_name syntax placed directly above a function definition is shorthand for func = decorator_name(func) — it's applied once, at definition time.

A correct decorator's wrapper function must accept *args, **kwargs (to transparently forward whatever arguments the original function is called with) and must return whatever the original function returns — a wrapper that calls the original but forgets to return its result silently discards the return value, a very common decorator bug.

content.heading: Arguments, Stacking, and Practical Examples
content.body: Multiple decorators can be stacked on one function; they apply bottom-up (the one closest to the function runs first, and its result is then passed to the next one up). Common real-world uses include logging (printing before/after a call), timing (measuring execution duration), caching (functools.lru_cache is a built-in decorator that memoizes results), access control (checking permissions before allowing a call), and retry logic. functools.wraps(func), applied to the wrapper function inside your decorator, preserves the original function's __name__ and docstring, which would otherwise be replaced by the wrapper's own — good practice for any decorator meant for general use.

content.explanation: @log_call is equivalent to add = log_call(add). wrapper forwards any arguments with *args/**kwargs and returns func's result, so add(2, 3) still behaves like addition with logging added around it.

keyPoints: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a (usually wrapping) function
@decorator above a function is shorthand for func = decorator(func)
A wrapper must accept *args, **kwargs and return the original function's result
functools.wraps preserves the original function's name/docstring on the wrapper
commonMistakes: Writing a wrapper that calls the original function but forgets to return its result
Forgetting *args, **kwargs, breaking the decorator for any function with arguments
Not using functools.wraps, so introspection tools and debuggers see the wrapper's identity instead of the original function's
